claims.text: Reflex roots: biceps (C5 and C6), radial brachialis (C6), triceps (C7), distal finger flexors (C8), quadriceps knee jerk (L4), ankle jerk (S1), jaw jerk (cranial nerve V).
claims.quote: Biceps (innervated by C5 and C6) Radial brachialis (C6) Triceps (C7) Distal finger flexors (C8) Quadriceps knee jerk (L4) Ankle jerk (S1) Jaw jerk (cranial nerve V)

claims.text: Lower vs upper motor neuron: lower motor neuron lesions (anterior horn cell, spinal root or peripheral nerve) depress reflexes; upper motor neuron lesions above the anterior horn cell increase them.
claims.quote: Lower motor neuron lesions (eg, affecting the anterior horn cell, spinal root, or peripheral nerve) depress reflexes; upper motor neuron lesions (ie, non–basal ganglia disorders anywhere above the anterior horn cell) increase reflexes.

claims.text: Jendrassik maneuver: augments hypoactive reflexes: the patient locks the hands and pulls them apart while a leg tendon is tapped (or pushes the knees together while an arm tendon is tested).
claims.quote: Jendrassik maneuver can be used to augment hypoactive reflexes: The patient locks the hands together and pulls vigorously apart as a tendon in the lower extremity is tapped. Alternatively, the patient can push the knees together against each other, while the upper limb tendon is tested.

claims.text: Plantar response: normal is flexion of the great toe; extension of the great toe with fanning of the other toes indicates spinal disinhibition from an upper motor neuron lesion.
claims.quote: Babinski, Chaddock, and Oppenheim reflexes all evaluate the plantar response. The normal reflex response is flexion of the great toe. An abnormal response is slower and consists of extension of the great toe with fanning of the other toes and often knee and hip flexion. This reaction is of spinal reflex origin and indicates spinal disinhibition due to an upper motor neuron lesion.

claims.text: Babinski technique: stroke the lateral sole firmly from the heel to the ball of the foot with a tongue blade or the end of a reflex hammer.
claims.quote: For Babinski reflex, the lateral sole of the foot is firmly stroked from the heel to the ball of the foot with a tongue blade or end of a reflex hammer.

claims.text: Hoffmann sign: flicking down on the nail of the third or fourth finger causes involuntary flexion of the distal phalanx of the thumb and index finger.
claims.quote: Hoffmann sign is present if flicking down on the nail on the third or fourth finger elicits involuntary flexion of the distal phalanx of the thumb and index finger.

claims.text: Clonus: tested by rapid dorsiflexion of the foot at the ankle; sustained clonus indicates an upper motor neuron disorder.
claims.quote: Testing for clonus (rhythmic, rapid alternation of muscle contraction and relaxation caused by sudden, passive tendon stretching) is done by rapid dorsiflexion of the foot at the ankle. Sustained clonus indicates an upper motor neuron disorder.

claims.text: Superficial abdominal reflex: lightly stroking the 4 quadrants near the umbilicus normally moves the umbilicus toward the stroke; depression may be from a central lesion, obesity or lax muscles, and absence may indicate spinal cord injury.
claims.quote: The superficial abdominal reflex is elicited by lightly stroking the 4 quadrants of the abdomen near the umbilicus with a wooden cotton applicator stick or similar tool. The normal response is contraction of the abdominal muscles causing the umbilicus to move toward the area being stroked. Stroking the skin toward the umbilicus is recommended to exclude the possibility that movement was caused by the skin being dragged by the stroking. Depression of this reflex may be due to a central lesion, obesity, or lax skeletal muscles (eg, after pregnancy); its absence may indicate spinal cord injury.

claims.text: Sphincter tone and anal wink: test S2 to S4: the patient squeezes the examiner’s gloved finger, or a light perianal touch contracts the external anal sphincter; rectal tone becomes lax in acute spinal cord injury or cauda equina syndrome.
claims.quote: To test sphincteric tone (S2 to S4 nerve root levels), the examiner inserts a gloved finger into the rectum and asks the patient to squeeze it. Alternatively, the perianal region is touched lightly with a cotton wisp; the normal response is contraction of the external anal sphincter (anal wink reflex). Rectal tone typically becomes lax in patients with acute spinal cord injury or cauda equine syndrome.

claims.text: Bulbospongiosus reflex: tests S2 to S4: tapping the dorsum of the penis normally contracts the bulbospongiosus muscle.
claims.quote: For the bulbospongiosus reflex, which tests S2 to S4 levels, the dorsum of the penis is tapped; normal response is contraction of the bulbospongiosus muscle.

claims.text: Cremasteric reflex: tests L2: stroking the medial thigh upward 7.6 cm (3 in) below the inguinal crease normally elevates the same-side testis.
claims.quote: For the cremasteric reflex, which tests the L2 level, the medial thigh 7.6 cm (3 in) below the inguinal crease is stroked upward; normal response is elevation of the ipsilateral testis.

claims.text: Strength grades (MRC): 0 no visible contraction; 1 visible contraction with no or trace movement; 2 movement but not against gravity; 3 against gravity but not resistance; 4 against some resistance; 5 full strength.
claims.quote: 0: No visible muscle contraction 1: Visible muscle contraction with no or trace movement 2: Limb movement, but not against gravity 3: Movement against gravity but not resistance 4: Movement against at least some resistance supplied by the examiner 5: Full strength

claims.text: Functional strength tests: rising from a squat or stepping onto a chair tests proximal leg strength; heel and toe walking test distal strength; pushing up with the arms to leave a chair indicates quadriceps weakness; climbing up the thighs to rise from supine (Gowers sign) suggests pelvic girdle weakness.
claims.quote: Rising from a squatting position or stepping onto a chair tests proximal leg strength; walking on the heels and on tiptoe tests distal strength. Pushing with the arms to get out of a chair indicates quadriceps weakness. Swinging the body to move the arms indicates shoulder girdle weakness. Rising from the supine position by turning prone, kneeling, and using the hands to climb up the thighs and slowly push erect (Gowers sign) suggests pelvic girdle weakness.

claims.text: Subtle weakness: decreased arm swing, pronator drift, less spontaneous use of a limb, an externally rotated leg, slow rapid alternating movements, or impaired fine dexterity.
claims.quote: Subtle weakness may be indicated by decreased arm swing while walking, pronator drift in an outstretched arm, decreased spontaneous use of a limb, an externally rotated leg, slowing of rapid alternating movements, or impairment of fine dexterity (eg, ability to fasten a button, open a safety pin, or remove a match from its box).

claims.text: Radiculopathy signs: muscles of the affected root become weak and atrophied (may be flaccid with fasciculations), sensory loss is dermatomal, segmental reflexes are diminished or absent, and electric shock–like pain radiates along the root.
claims.quote: Muscles innervated by the affected motor root become weak and atrophy; they also may be flaccid with fasciculations. Sensory root involvement causes sensory impairment in a dermatomal distribution. Corresponding segmental deep tendon reflexes may be diminished or absent. Electric shock–like pains may radiate along the affected nerve root’s distribution.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Nerve Root Disorders

claims.text: Root pain triggers: moving the spine, coughing, sneezing or the Valsalva maneuver can worsen it.
claims.quote: Pain may be exacerbated by movements that transmit pressure to the nerve root through the subarachnoid space (eg, moving the spine, coughing, sneezing, doing the Valsalva maneuver).
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Nerve Root Disorders

claims.text: C4 root: pain in the lower neck and trapezius area with paresthesias of the lower neck and upper shoulder girdle.
claims.quote: C4 Pain in the lower neck and trapezius area with paresthesias involving the lower neck and upper shoulder girdle
claims.locator: Table: Symptoms of Common Radiculopathies by Cord Level

claims.text: L3 root: pain, numbness and paresthesias in the anterior and medial thigh and knee, quadriceps weakness and a diminished patellar reflex.
claims.quote: L3 Pain, numbness, and paresthesias in the anterior and medial thigh and knee with quadriceps weakness and diminished patellar reflex
claims.locator: Table: Symptoms of Common Radiculopathies by Cord Level

claims.text: Spinal cord compression findings: a sensory level, flaccid paraparesis or quadriparesis, reflex changes below the compression (early hyporeflexia, later hyperreflexia) and sphincter dysfunction.
claims.quote: Findings indicating spinal cord compression include the following: A sensory level (an abrupt change in sensation below a horizontal line across the spine) Flaccid paraparesis or quadriparesis Reflex abnormalities below the site of compression Early-onset hyporeflexia followed later by hyperreflexia Sphincter dysfunction
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Nerve Root Disorders

claims.text: Cauda equina syndrome: bilateral leg weakness in muscles supplied by L3 through S1, sensory loss often in the saddle area, and bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction (urinary retention or incontinence, loss of rectal tone, abnormal bulbocavernosus and anal wink reflexes).
claims.quote: Cauda equina syndrome (like conus medullaris syndrome) causes bilateral leg weakness in muscles supplied by L3 through S1 and sensory loss in the distribution of the affected nerve roots (often in the saddle area), as well as bladder, bowel, and pudendal dysfunction (eg, urinary retention, urinary frequency, urinary or fecal incontinence, erectile dysfunction, loss of rectal tone, abnormal bulbocavernosus and anal wink reflexes). Urinary retention or incontinence results from loss of sphincter function.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Cauda Equina Syndrome

claims.text: Cauda equina vs cord injury: leg tone and reflexes are decreased in cauda equina syndrome (unlike subacute or chronic cord injury), but a severe acute cord injury also starts with decreased tone and reflexes (spinal shock).
claims.quote: In cauda equina syndrome (unlike in subacute or chronic spinal cord injury), muscle tone and deep tendon reflexes are decreased in the legs. However, if an acute spinal cord injury is severe, muscle tone and deep tendon reflexes are initially decreased or absent (spinal shock), making distinguishing it from cauda equina syndrome difficult soon after injury.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Cauda Equina Syndrome

claims.text: Cauda equina cause: most often a herniated disc in the lumbar spine.
claims.quote: Cauda equina syndrome most commonly results from a herniated disc in the lumbar spine.

claims.text: Cauda equina imaging: when suspected, MRI immediately if available; CT myelography if MRI is unavailable.
claims.quote: If symptoms suggest cauda equina syndrome, MRI should be done immediately if available. If MRI is unavailable, CT myelography should be done.
